concepts.title: When Wages Rose, Why Did the Basics Cost More?
concepts.description:
A London labourer's daily wage more than doubled between the early 1500s and early 1600s. Yet a reconstructed basket of basic needs took more days' pay to cover. This illustrated history follows the changing cost of bread, fuel, soap, light and other essentials from before the Black Death to the late 19th century—and explains why a rising wage could still lose ground to prices. The figures are historical estimates expressed as wage-day equivalents, not records of a family's actual work year or a comparison with modern living costs.

#CostOfLiving #EconomicHistory #PaperDetour
concepts.audience_surface: Viewers curious about everyday economics and historical change; YouTube long-form home and search surfaces.
concepts.promise: Explain the counterintuitive period when daily pay rose sharply but the modeled basic basket became harder to cover relative to that pay.
concepts.genre_mood: Historical economic investigation; curious, tactile, measured, with a reversal.
concepts.first_confirmation: The intro defines the wage-day measure and the modeled family basket; later the 1500–1549 comparison gives about 176 wage-days.
concepts.payoff: For 1600–1649 the estimate is about 216 wage-days; prices rose faster than the silver wage. The late 19th-century estimate falls to about 116.
concepts.likely_misreading: Could be read as modern inflation advice or proof of actual annual household workdays.
concepts.hook: A single oversized silver coin is split by a rising paper wage ribbon while a basket of necessities stays just out of reach; the unexpected relationship is visible without implying exact coin prices.

brief.prompt: Create one complete 16:9 handmade paper/card diorama thumbnail for a historical London cost-of-living investigation. First glance: one oversized silver-colored wage coin under a rising paper wage ribbon, while a small but clearly recognizable bread-and-fuel basket is pushed farther beyond it, making the counterintuitive question visible. Use a bold low camera angle, physical layered edges and a strong warm/cool light split; direct attention from the rising ribbon down to the basket with a cut-paper diagonal. Include the exact large rounded paper lettering: ‘MORE PAY. LESS BUY.’ Keep only bread, a fuel bundle and a candle as supporting necessities. Rich tactile fibers, thickness, folds and contact shadows; no glossy CGI, modern coinage, modern prices, charts, logos, realistic documentary photo, or implied exact household bills. The metaphor must read as a model of relative purchasing power, not a literal event. Thumbnail QA title context: ‘When Wages Rose, Why Did the Basics Cost More?’ At 320×180 the coin, upward ribbon, basket and words must remain immediately legible.
brief.visual_intent: A price-versus-wage reversal: the gaze travels from the rising wage ribbon to the basket that remains costly relative to it. Verify the relationship and exact title at 320×180; the text is a separate concise hook.

concepts.title: How Many Days' Wages Bought the Basics?
concepts.description:
Bread, fuel, soap and light: how much of a London labourer's modeled year's earnings would the basics consume? This illustrated history turns a reconstructed basket into wage-days and follows the estimate from before the Black Death through the 19th century. The answer does not move in a straight line: it improves, reverses as prices outrun pay, then improves again. These are model-based historical comparisons, not observed work schedules or a measure of modern living costs.

#CostOfLiving #LondonHistory #PaperDetour
concepts.audience_surface: Viewers drawn to a concrete everyday question; YouTube long-form home and suggested surfaces.
concepts.promise: Make the labor-time cost of a defined basket tangible and reveal its uneven change across centuries.
concepts.genre_mood: Material, human-scale historical explainer; inquisitive and empathetic.
concepts.first_confirmation: The intro names bread, fuel, soap, candles and a small housing allowance, and explains that wage-days are a model conversion.
concepts.payoff: The sequence moves from about 176 to 216 to 116 wage-days for selected periods, showing an early modern reversal and later improvement.
concepts.likely_misreading: The scene might imply a documented family shopping event, fixed actual annual bill or exact allocation of a worker's time.
concepts.hook: An oversized hand holds one coin above a divided paper basket; bread, soap and candle are visible while the coin's shadow falls short, staging the intro's specific necessities.

brief.prompt: Create one complete 16:9 handmade paper/card diorama thumbnail for a historical London labourer's cost-of-living story. Build the scene around the intro's concrete necessities: a large hand holds one silver-colored wage coin above a divided paper basket containing bread, a small fuel bundle, soap and a candle. Let the coin's long shadow fall short of the basket, a clear metaphor for the question of how much work the basics cost. Direct the eye from hand to coin to basket; use a dramatic close-up and layered cut-paper depth, rich fibers, thickness and contact shadows. Add exact large rounded paper lettering: ‘WHAT DOES A YEAR COST?’ The basket is a reconstruction, not a real family's documented inventory; avoid exact price labels, modern coins, extra goods, modern props, logos, photo realism or glossy CGI. Thumbnail QA title context: ‘How Many Days' Wages Bought the Basics?’ At 320×180 preserve readable text and the hand-coin-basket relation.
brief.visual_intent: Intro-linked object/action concept: a hand, wage coin and defined necessities establish the premise in one glance. Check that the shortfall reads as a question about modeled affordability, not a literal documented transaction; verify at 320×180.

concepts.title: The Centuries When Necessities Took More Work
concepts.description:
A reconstructed basket of basic needs could take fewer or more days' pay depending on the period. In London, selected wage and price estimates show an unexpected early modern setback: daily silver wages rose from the 1500s to the 1600s, but the basket's wage-day cost increased. Follow the measure from before the Black Death to the late 1800s, with its assumptions and limits made clear. This is a historical model, not a complete household budget or a modern cost comparison.

#EconomicHistory #Wages #PaperDetour
concepts.audience_surface: Viewers interested in long-term living standards and historical reversals; YouTube search and suggested surfaces.
concepts.promise: Trace the periods when necessities became easier or harder to cover relative to a daily wage.
concepts.genre_mood: Reflective historical investigation; tension at the reversal, then a qualified resolution.
concepts.first_confirmation: The opening sets the before-plague shortfall and explains the model's assumed 250 paid days and 5% rent allowance.
concepts.payoff: The threshold turns at the 1600s comparison: about 216 wage-days versus about 176 in the preceding selected period, followed by about 116 in 1850–1899.
concepts.likely_misreading: A split scene could suggest a neat, continuous trend or claim a single cause for nineteenth-century change.
concepts.hook: A thick paper threshold divides two comparable basket-and-wage scenes; a large path of paper day-markers crosses upward at the middle period, then descends later.

brief.prompt: Create one complete 16:9 handmade paper/card diorama thumbnail for a historical London cost-of-living investigation. Show a thick, physical cut-paper threshold dividing three clearly related eras in one continuous handcrafted scene: on left a necessities basket sits near a daily wage token, at center the same-sized basket sits farther beyond the token, and at right it sits closer again. Use a bold stepped line of paper day-markers that rises at the center and falls on the right; keep baskets and tokens comparable in scale so perspective does not falsely imply the historical difference. The first glance should register a reversal, not a smooth upward trend. Add exact large rounded paper lettering: ‘THE PRICE WENT UP’. Tactile layered edges, folds, fibers and contact shadows; no exact numeric chart, dates, modern currency, logos, glossy CGI, or claim that the 19th-century change has one cause. Thumbnail QA title context: ‘The Centuries When Necessities Took More Work’. At 320×180, threshold, central rise and short text must remain readable.
brief.visual_intent: A material threshold dramatizes the non-linear movement in selected model estimates. Check that baskets and wage tokens stay comparable and that it does not imply a continuous trend or explain the later improvement causally.
